concept.name: Simple return
concept.definition: The fractional change in value of an investment over a single period: the difference between final and initial value divided by the initial value, including any income such as dividends in the final value. It is the standard per-period return measure in empirical finance.
concept.intuition: It answers 'by what percentage did my money grow this period?' A 5% simple return means $100 became $105.
concept.mechanics: Divide the change in value (final plus distributions minus initial) by the initial value. Simple returns aggregate across assets by value-weighted averaging (portfolio return is the weighted sum of asset returns) but compound, not add, across time.
concept.formula: R_t = (V_t + D_t - V_{t-1}) / V_{t-1}, where V_t is the end-of-period value, V_{t-1} the initial value, and D_t any distributions (dividends, interest) received during the period.
concept.failure_modes: Simple returns do not add across time - summing them over multiple periods overstates compounded growth when returns are volatile. They are also bounded below by -100%, which complicates symmetric statistical models.
concept.misconceptions: A +50% gain followed by a -50% loss does not net to zero: (1.5)(0.5) = 0.75, a 25% cumulative loss. Arithmetic averaging of simple returns is not the rate at which capital actually compounds.
concept.example: A stock bought at $100 that pays a $2 dividend and ends the period at $105 has simple return R = (105 + 2 - 100)/100 = 7%.
